lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Call it the Six Day War and you picture six days of fighting. Tanks grinding across three fronts, cities changing hands, a war fought and refought in the field.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: At seven forty five in the morning on June fifth, nineteen sixty seven, roughly one hundred and eighty Israeli jets crossed the Mediterranean below Egyptian radar and struck eleven airfields at once.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Within three hours, about three hundred of Egypt's four hundred and twenty combat aircraft were burning on the ground. The pilots who were supposed to defend Cairo never left the tarmac.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The war was decided before most of the Arab world even knew it had begun. Everything that followed for the next five days was a land campaign against an enemy that no longer had an air force.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Six Day War. June fifth to the tenth, nineteen sixty seven.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The countdown starts three weeks earlier, with Egypt.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On May fourteenth, President Gamal Abdel Nasser moves Egyptian divisions into the Sinai Peninsula. Two days later he demands the withdrawal of the United Nations force that has patrolled the border for a decade, and U Thant complies within days.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On May twenty second, Nasser closes the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping, cutting the route most of Israel's oil comes through. Israel had said back in nineteen fifty seven that closing the Straits would be treated as an act of war.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On May thirtieth, King Hussein of Jordan flies to Cairo and places his own army under Egyptian command. Israel, nine miles wide at its narrowest point, now faces three armies on three fronts.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Inside Israel, the three weeks in between have a name. Ha-hamtana, the waiting.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Reservists sit in the Negev with nothing to do but wait for orders. Rabbis consecrate parks in Tel Aviv as emergency cemeteries. Hotels clear their basements for casualties that have not happened yet.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: This is a generation that buried Europe's Jews two decades earlier, now watching three armies mobilize on its borders.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On June first, four days before the strike, Moshe Dayan is appointed defense minister.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The cabinet, led by Prime Minister Levi Eshkol, debates for days. Then it chooses to strike first.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Four days before that cabinet decision, Nasser had already told Arab trade unionists in Cairo what he believed this was.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: We are confronting Israel and the West as well, the West which created Israel and which despised us Arabs. Our basic objective will be the destruction of Israel. The Arab people want to fight.

segments.author: Gamal Abdel Nasser
segments.work: Speech to the General Council of the International Confederation of Arab Trade Unions, Cairo

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: For a state founded by Holocaust survivors, these were not abstract words. They were why parks were already being consecrated as cemeteries.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: By June tenth, Israel holds the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip, taken from Egypt. It holds the West Bank and East Jerusalem, taken from Jordan. It holds the Golan Heights, taken from Syria.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The land under Israeli control grows from about twenty thousand seven hundred square kilometers to roughly sixty nine thousand, more than three times its previous size, in one hundred and thirty two hours.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On June seventh, Israeli paratroopers reach the Western Wall in Jerusalem's old city for the first time in nineteen years. A photograph of three soldiers looking up at the stone becomes the war's defining image.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Between fifteen thousand and twenty thousand Arab soldiers die. Many of them are Egyptian conscripts who walk into the Sinai desert without water after their own officers have already fled.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Israel loses between seven hundred and seventy six and nine hundred and eighty three.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The killing runs in one direction only.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The day after the strike, Israel's foreign minister Abba Eban stood before the UN Security Council and put the choice in the starkest terms available to him.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: The choice for Israel was to live or to perish, to defend the national existence or to forfeit it for all time.

segments.author: Abba Eban
segments.work: Address to the UN Security Council

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On the sixth day, an estimated one million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza wake up under military occupation. That occupation is given no end date. In twenty twenty six it is fifty nine years old.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Fifteen years later, one of the men who made the decision to strike first stood up in public and said something that did not fit the story his own country told about that week.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In August nineteen eighty two, Prime Minister Menachem Begin addressed Israel's National Defense College.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: In June, nineteen sixty seven, we again had a choice. The Egyptian army concentrations in the Sinai approaches did not prove that Nasser was really about to attack us. We must be honest with ourselves. We decided to attack him.

segments.author: Menachem Begin
segments.work: Address to Israel's National Defense College

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Whether Israel struck to survive or struck because it could is the question this war left open. Five accounts answer it five different ways, each one in its own terms first.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: This account begins with the siege, not the strike.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A hundred thousand Egyptian troops and about nine hundred tanks in Sinai. The United Nations force gone at Nasser's own request. The Straits of Tiran closed, an act Israel had named in advance as grounds for war. Jordan's army handed to an Egyptian general.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Cairo's own state radio was broadcasting that the hour of Israel's destruction had come. For a country nine miles wide at its narrowest, with no room to absorb a first blow, pre-emption was not aggression. It was the only form of self-defense available.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The capture of Jerusalem's old city, Israeli soldiers reaching the Western Wall for the first time in nineteen years, is remembered in this account as a homecoming, not a conquest.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Abba Eban put the government's own calculation in five words.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: We knew that our limit of safety had been reached, and perhaps passed.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: This account says the war was a bluff that got out of hand.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A false Soviet report told Cairo that Israel was massing troops against Syria. Nasser could not be seen abandoning an ally, so he moved forces into Sinai as a show of resolve, aimed as much at rivals in Amman and Riyadh as at Israel. His own generals privately doubted the army was ready for a real war.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Closing the Straits was the act of a leader who had climbed too high to climb back down. He expected a political crisis, not a first strike that would erase his air force in one morning.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Two days before the trade union speech that named Israel's destruction as an objective, Nasser had told a Cairo press conference something closer to what he said he actually intended.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: We are ready for war. Our armed forces, our people, all of us are ready for war, but we shall in no way be the ones to begin.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In Arabic this is called al-Naksa, the setback. For this account, nineteen sixty seven was not six days. It was the start of a condition that has never ended.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Roughly three hundred thousand people are displaced from the West Bank and Gaza. About a hundred and seventy five thousand of them are made refugees for the second time in nineteen years.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: For the one million who stay, June tenth brings military rule. Permits to build, permits to travel, permits to dig a well. Land declared state property. The first settlement goes up at Kfar Etzion that September.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In the village of Beit Nuba, in the Latrun salient, the record does not give a name to the family that told an interviewer what happened to their home.

lines.speaker: F
lines.text: We were told to leave for a few days until the fighting stopped. We are still waiting to go back.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Declassified Israeli, American, and Soviet records let historians check what the decision makers actually knew in May, and it does not match the memory of a country facing extinction.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Both Israeli military intelligence and the American CIA assessed, before the war, that Nasser was not about to attack, and that if war came Israel would win it inside two weeks. President Johnson was told the same thing.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Begin's own nineteen eighty two speech, the one already heard in this episode, is the most cited piece of evidence for this account. He called it a choice, not a necessity.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Yitzhak Rabin, who directed the campaign as chief of staff, said something close to that to a French newspaper the following year.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: I do not believe that Nasser wanted war. The two divisions he sent into Sinai would not have been enough to unleash an offensive against Israel. He knew it and we knew it.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The war ended in six days. The diplomacy it started is still unfinished fifty nine years later.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: United Nations Security Council Resolution two forty two, adopted unanimously that November, calls for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from territories occupied in the conflict, paired with the right of every state in the region to live within secure and recognized boundaries.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The English text left out the word the before territories, on purpose, so Israel could read it as withdrawal from some land and the Arab states could read it as withdrawal from all of it.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Lord Caradon, the British ambassador who drafted it, admitted years later exactly what he had done.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: We did not say there should be withdrawal to the sixty seven line. We did not put the word the into it. We did not say all the territories, deliberately.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The resolution mentions the Palestinians only once, and only as a refugee problem to be settled justly, never as a people with a claim of their own.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And here is what each one needs the listener not to notice.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Israeli account stops at the border of its own victory. Intelligence had already judged that Nasser was not about to attack. Fifteen years later Begin himself called it a choice. And it has no room in it for the occupation and the settlements that followed.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Nasserist account leaves out that its own leader had named the destruction of Israel as an objective in his own words, that closing the Straits was a recognized ground for war, and that three armies really were mobilized against a country nine miles wide.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Palestinian account says little about the Arab governments whose mobilization brought the war on, or about the nineteen years the West Bank had already spent under Jordanian rule before this war, with no Palestinian state then either.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The revisionist account is written with hindsight that nobody living through May of nineteen sixty seven possessed. It has little to say about the terror on an Israeli street that could not read a classified cable, or about a rhetoric of annihilation that a country of Holocaust survivors had every reason to take literally.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And the diplomatic account, fluent in the ambiguity of a single missing word, has almost nothing to say about the one million people that ambiguity was drafted over.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The occupation that began on June tenth never ended. In twenty twenty six it is fifty nine years old.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The refugee population it created, added to the one from nineteen forty eight, now exceeds five point nine million people registered with the United Nations.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In the Latrun salient, the villages of Imwas, Yalu, and Beit Nuba were bulldozed within weeks of the ceasefire. Their ruins were later planted over as a public park.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: It is called Canada Park. The picnic tables sit on the foundations of the houses.
